rendered:
The review does not really recommend tens of nanometres for low-diffusivity oxides. Tens of nanometres is what the literature typically reports, because thickness is hard to control with easily scalable processes. The review's own recommendation is a much thinner layer, below about ten nanometers[1], and its reasoning is as follows.

First, the literature reports thicknesses of this order because they are difficult to control with scalable processes.[2]

Second, the review states that the lithium-ion diffusivity of most oxides and fluorides is extremely low, particularly for ZrO2, and it uses diffusion time (diffusion length squared over diffusivity, with diffusivities taken from its diffusivity table) to judge coating thickness.[3] Because of this, longer diffusion times are obtained for thicker layers.[4] The review concludes that the measured performance appears limited by ionic diffusion through the coating, so the ideal thickness is below about ten nanometers[5] for better electrochemical performance.[6]

Third, the general guidance is that the most widely used cost-effective, scalable coatings have very low lithium-ion diffusivity, so their maximum thickness is recommended at around ∼10 nm[7] to use the benefits of the coating.[8]

Fourth, a further reason to keep ZrO2 layers thin is that inert, stable coatings such as ZrO2 may react with lithium ions and form secondary phases, which causes capacity fading.[9]

So thin layers keep lithium-ion transport through the low-diffusivity coating short while limiting side reactions.
